## Conclusion

There is no general productivity penalty for remote work; there is a penalty for particular kinds of work, and the studies disagree mainly because they measure different jobs [1][2][3]. Output per hour holds up or improves where tasks decompose into independent units, and falls where the work depends on dense, unscheduled coordination [2][4]. The strongest opposing view is that the individual-output measures used in the favourable studies miss the part that degrades — the slow erosion of cross-team information flow, which shows up in network measures rather than in call counts — and it has real support [4], so the conclusion here is limited to measured output over the horizons these studies observe. Read as a claim about a whole firm over years rather than a worker over months, "reduces productivity" is not settled by anything below.

## Key findings

- A randomised trial at a Chinese travel agency found a 13 percent performance increase among call-centre staff working from home, roughly two-thirds from more minutes worked per shift — fewer breaks and sick days — and one-third from more calls per minute [1].
- A study of IT professionals at a large firm found total hours worked rose while output did not, so output per hour fell — the opposite sign to [1] on a job that looks superficially similar [2].
- Call-centre workers at a large US retailer answered about 12 percent fewer calls per hour when remote, a result usually attributed to how the two firms selected workers into remote status [3].
- Firm-wide remote work made collaboration networks more static and more siloed, with fewer bridging ties across teams [4].
- Working from home settled well above its pre-2020 level and below its 2020 peak, so the steady state being measured is hybrid rather than fully remote [5].

## The strongest counterargument

The serious objection is not that remote workers slack. It is that the favourable evidence measures the wrong thing. Bloom et al. and the retailer study both score individual throughput on tasks with a clean output metric [1][3], and Gibbs, Mengel and Siemroth show that even there the metric can move against remote work once hours are counted properly [2]. Yang et al. add the part none of them capture: after a firm-wide shift, collaboration networks became more siloed and fewer ties bridged groups [4]. Information flow of that kind does not appear in this quarter's output; it appears later, in work that never got started because two people never spoke.

For the conclusion to flip, that mechanism would have to be shown to reduce measured output at the firm level over a horizon long enough for the network effect to bite. Yang et al. document the network change but do not price it [4], and no source here follows a firm long enough to. The conclusion above is accordingly stated about measured output over the observed horizons, and it should not be read as a claim about firm performance a decade out.

## What the measurement studies show

Bloom et al. randomised call-centre staff at a Chinese travel agency into home and office work and found a 13 percent performance increase for the home group, decomposing into more minutes worked per shift and more calls per minute [1]. The design is the strongest in this literature, and the job is also the most decomposable in it.

Gibbs, Mengel and Siemroth complicate the picture using personnel and analytics data on IT professionals. Hours worked rose after the shift home while output was roughly flat, which is a decline in output per hour on a job that involves substantially more coordination than answering calls [2]. Emanuel and Harrington, working with a large US retailer's call centres, report remote workers answering about 12 percent fewer calls per hour — opposite in sign to [1] on nearly the same task, which is why selection is the usual explanation offered for the pair [3].

## Why the results diverge

Task composition accounts for most of the disagreement. Work that decomposes into independent units survives distribution well; work requiring rapid, low-latency negotiation between people does not, because that negotiation moves onto channels that impose a scheduling cost [2][4].

Selection accounts for much of the rest. Studies in which workers chose remote status measure the choice as much as the arrangement, and firms that moved everyone at once in 2020 measured a shock rather than a steady state [3][5].
